snapshot.exam_hook: ⚡ TNPSC GS Hook: NE Monsoon: TN Rain. SW Monsoon: India Rain. May: Hot. Oct-Dec: Retreating. Kerala: 1st Rain.

quick_notes.title: Climate of India
quick_notes.detail: Tropical Monsoon Climate. 4 seasons: Winter (Jan-Feb), Summer (Mar-May), SW Monsoon (Jun-Sep), NE Monsoon (Oct-Dec).
quick_notes.explanation: India has a Tropical Monsoon Climate, which means the weather is generally hot and is strongly controlled by seasonal winds called monsoons that bring heavy rain. The word tropical means the country lies near the equator, so it stays warm all year, and monsoon refers to the wind pattern that reverses direction between summer and winter. India experiences four main seasons: Winter from January to February, which is cool and dry; Summer from March to May, which is very hot and dry; the Southwest Monsoon from June to September, when winds from the southwest bring most of the country's rainfall; and the Northeast Monsoon from October to December, when winds from the northeast bring rain mainly to the southeastern coast. The Southwest Monsoon is the most important because it provides the water needed for farming and drinking across most of India. The Northeast Monsoon is weaker and only affects a smaller area, like Tamil Nadu.

quick_notes.title: SW Monsoon
quick_notes.detail: Enters via Kerala (June). Two branches : Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal. Provides 75% rain to India.
quick_notes.explanation: The Southwest Monsoon is the main rainy season for India, bringing about 75 percent of the country's total annual rainfall. It begins when moist winds from the Indian Ocean move toward the land, entering India through the coast of Kerala in the month of June. These winds split into two separate streams called branches: the Arabian Sea branch flows along the western coast, and the Bay of Bengal branch moves up the eastern side of the country. The Arabian Sea branch is responsible for heavy rain on the western coast, while the Bay of Bengal branch brings rain to the northeastern states and the Gangetic plains. Together, these two branches distribute the monsoon rains across most of India, making this season crucial for farming and water supplies.

quick_notes.title: NE Monsoon (Retreating)
quick_notes.detail: Primary source of rain for Tamil Nadu (Oct-Dec). TN gets ~48% of its annual rain from here.
quick_notes.explanation: The Northeast Monsoon, also called the Retreating Monsoon, is the main source of rain for Tamil Nadu from October to December. The word "monsoon" means a seasonal wind that changes direction and brings rain. During this time, winds blow from the northeast over the Bay of Bengal, picking up moisture and dropping it on the eastern coast of India, especially Tamil Nadu. Tamil Nadu gets about 48 percent of its total rain for the whole year from this monsoon season. This happens because the southwest monsoon winds, which bring rain to most of India from June to September, start to weaken and pull back, or retreat, toward the south, changing direction to come from the northeast. So, while other parts of India are dry in October, Tamil Nadu receives its heaviest rainfall during these three months.

quick_notes.title: Tamil Nadu Climate
quick_notes.detail: Tropical Maritime. Hottest : May (Agni Nakshatram). Rainiest : Nov (NE Monsoon).
quick_notes.explanation: Tamil Nadu has a tropical maritime climate, which means the weather is generally hot and humid because the state is near the sea. The hottest month is May, and this period is locally called Agni Nakshatram, which means "fire star" and refers to the intense heat. The rainiest month is November, when the state receives most of its rainfall from the Northeast Monsoon, or NE Monsoon, which is a wind pattern that brings rain from the northeast direction during the winter season.

quick_notes.title: Agri-Climatic Zones
quick_notes.detail: TN is divided into 7 zones. Focus on Cauvery Delta and Western zones.
quick_notes.explanation: Agri-Climatic Zones are specific areas within a state that have similar weather, soil, and farming conditions. Tamil Nadu (TN) is divided into 7 such zones. The Cauvery Delta Zone is the region around the Cauvery River where the soil is very fertile and water is plentiful, making it the main area for growing rice. The Western Zone covers the districts along the western side of Tamil Nadu, like Coimbatore and Erode, which have a drier climate and are known for crops like cotton, sugarcane, and oilseeds. Each zone is defined by its unique combination of rainfall, temperature, and soil type, which determines which crops can be grown there successfully.
